title: Dragon Ball Z theme park, financed by Saudi Arabia, to be built in France
description: “You know of my interest in mangas,” says French president. It’s unusual for a single franchise to get an entire theme park of its own. Disneyland, of course, is a place for not only the Disney animated catalog, but also the various live-action properties the company now holds the rights to, such as Star Wars […]
content:
“You know of my interest in mangas,” says French president.

It’s unusual for a single franchise to get an entire theme park of its own. Disneyland, of course, is a place for not only the Disney animated catalog, but also the various live-action properties the company now holds the rights to, such as Star Wars and the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Universal Studios’ attractions cover a wide variety of Hollywood movies, plus Nintendo’s Super Mario and a handful of other video game and anime IPs. Even Ghibli Park is a place for the celebration of the studio’s overall output, not one specific film.

But there’s a dedicated Dragon Ball Z theme park on the way, though it’ll be opening on the opposite side of the hemisphere from the anime/manga’s home country.

The office of French president Emmanuel Macron has announced that a Dragon Ball Z theme park will be built in the suburbs of Paris. The facility will be one of three new theme parks to be developed in Cergy-Pontoise, roughly 45 minutes northwest of downtown Paris, which will ostensibly sit on the site of the former Mirapolis, an amusement park which closed in 1991.

This news might have jogged your memory that there’s also a Dragon Ball Z theme park in development in Saudi Arabia, and the French park will also be built with Saudi money. The three-park project, with a total budget of 6 billion Euros, (roughly US$7 billion), is being spearheaded by Qiddiya Investment Company, a Saudi government fund with crown prince and prime minister Mohammed bin Salman as its chairman. Talks for the French Dragon Ball Z park began a year and a half ago, when Macron and bin Salman found out they had a shared love for Dragon Ball Z, and the announcement of the French park was timed to coincide with bin Salman’s latest visit to Paris.

Posting to his official Twitter account, Macron said “You know of my interest in mangas. You are also aware of my determination to attract investments in France that will create employment and make the most ambitious projects possible,” while claiming that the parks will create 22,000 new jobs (for comparison, Oriental Land, the company that manages Tokyo Disneyland, Disney Sea, and its associated hotels, currently employs around 27,000 people). Macron expressed his gratitude with “Thank you to Qiddiya and to Saudi Arabia for your confidence in our country, our talents, and our future.”

As for when that Dragon Ball Z-ified future is coming, there’s currently no timetable for the Franch park’s opening, but given the size of the project, it’s probably going to be at least a few years until it’s ready to start receiving guests, which should give Macron more time to practice his Kamehameha pose.

Source: Jiji, Asahi Shimbun, Reuters, Oriental Land Company, Twitter/@EmmanuelMacron

title: Japan tripled its departure tax to fund tourism but is using the money on cherry blossoms and bears
description: Questions are being raised over whether money from foreign tourists is being used as intended. On 1 July, Japan increased its departure tax for everyone flying out of the country, raising it from 1,000 yen (US$6.28) to 3,000 yen per departure, with the cost included in the price of the airfare. While the threefold increase […]
content:
Questions are being raised over whether money from foreign tourists is being used as intended.

On 1 July, Japan increased its departure tax for everyone flying out of the country, raising it from 1,000 yen (US$6.28) to 3,000 yen per departure, with the cost included in the price of the airfare. While the threefold increase applies to both foreign tourists and Japanese citizens, the government acknowledged that most of the additional revenue would be collected from overseas visitors, estimating they would contribute around 646 billion yen (US$4.05 billion) this year, compared to roughly 164 billion yen from Japanese citizens.

To soften the blow, the government told the public that the extra revenue would go back into travel-related initiatives, like lowering passport fees for Japanese citizens, and funding programs to combat overtourism, including the promotion of lesser-known parts of Japan. However, it was revealed this week that the 2026 fiscal budget, which was approved in April before the higher departure tax came into effect, also allocated departure tax revenue to cover the costs of bear control and pest prevention for cherry blossom trees – measures that are largely aimed at protecting the lives and environment of people living in Japan rather than improving the experience of foreign visitors.

According to Japanese media reports, the government allocated 6.2 billion yen for bear-related countermeasures in the 2026 fiscal year, with 6 billion yen of that amount coming from departure tax revenue. A newly created 600 million-yen budget for pest control of sakura trees is reportedly being funded entirely by the departure tax.

The Environment Ministry has justified the spending, saying that foreign visitors could benefit from countermeasures against bears, and many people from abroad come to Japan specifically to see the cherry blossoms.

▼ Foreign tourists aren’t the only people who enjoy the blossoms, though, as locals flock to see them too.

Bear encounters have become an increasingly serious issue in Japan, with both local residents and foreign tourists sustaining injuries from the animals, including at tourist spots. However, after news of the allocations came to light this week, questions have been raised over whether the heavy funding of bear and sakura pest control aligns with the original intention of the increased tax, which was introduced to fund tourism-related initiatives.

It’s also important to note that bear control and cherry blossom tree pest prevention measures had traditionally been funded from the government’s general budget, which draws on taxes such as income and corporate tax without being restricted to a particular use. Those defending the new funding argue that money from the general budget can now be used to cover other costs, but it’s unclear where the resulting funds will be redirected.

In light of these revelations, and amid growing concerns from the public, Japan’s Minister of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism, Yasushi Kaneko, announced on 25 August that the government would consider reviewing how the money is allocated. He said the government would examine the spending carefully and work to ensure the money is directed towards projects with greater effectiveness and without raising concerns.

With tourism-related initiatives covering such a broad spectrum of issues that affect everyday life in Japan, it’s quite possible for the government to justify any use of funds if it has the slightest connection to tourism. As the government aims to increase the number of annual foreign visitors from over 40 million in 2025 to 60 million by 2030, the revenue collected from the departure tax is set to rise with it, making responsible use of funds even more vital to ensuring that the problems of overtourism don’t get lost amid concerns over sakura pests and bears.

Sources: Asahi Shimbun (1, 2) via Yahoo! News Japan (1, 2)

title: Amid foreign sex tourist rise, Japanese government considering outlawing paying for prostitution
description: No selling should also mean no buying, expert panel says. Common sense would suggest that if there’s something that’s been judged as unacceptable enough within a society for there to be a blanket ban on its sale, that buying it should be illegal too, right? Like, if the law says that “Under no circumstances can […]
content:
No selling should also mean no buying, expert panel says.

Common sense would suggest that if there’s something that’s been judged as unacceptable enough within a society for there to be a blanket ban on its sale, that buying it should be illegal too, right? Like, if the law says that “Under no circumstances can Godzilla eggs be sold,” it doesn’t seem like there’s any logical scenario in which it would be OK to purchase them.

And yet, in one of the many ways that Godzilla eggs and sexual intercourse are different, the Japanese legal system doesn’t handle buying sex the same as it does selling sex, as one is explicitly outlawed, and the other carries no legal penalty whatsoever. That loophole could be closing soon, though, and foreign tourists might be playing a role in the proposed revision.

Under Japan’s current Prostitution Prevention Law, only the selling of intercourse is treated as a criminal act. So if Person A pays Person B for a role in the hay, Person B is looking at up to six months in jail or a fine of up to 20,000 yen (US$125) if they get caught. Meanwhile, Person A hasn’t broken any law, and therefore faces no legal repercussion as long as they didn’t commit any other wrongdoing (such as sex with a minor, coercion, or physical assault).

As we discussed earlier this year, the Japanese government’s Ministry of Justice has come to feel like this imbalance is both unfair and ineffective, and assembled a panel of experts to discuss what changes need to be made. This week, the panel previewed its recommendations in a draft report, in which it says the members are in consensus that prostitution purchasers should be punished as well.

The proposal follows recent attempts by Tokyo’s Shinjuku Ward to reduce prostitution within its section of the city, which includes the Kabukicho entertainment and red light district. Since the end of the pandemic, there’s been a noticeable increase in the number of streetwalkers on roads near a park and love hotel district close to Shinjuku Station. Ward administrators say that social media videos showing women loitering on the streets as they wait for customers looking to purchase sex have been attracting increasing amounts of attention overseas, leading to an increase in foreign tourists coming to the area to purchase the prostitutes’ services themselves or to gawk at the selection on display. In response, local citizens’ groups have begun public awareness patrols broadcasting announcements that “Prostitution is a crime” in both Japanese and English.

Though not the sole impetus for the proposed revisions, an unwanted increase in foreign sex tourists is one more reason to tighten the law. In addition to introducing penalties for purchasers, some on the panel also recommend raising the penalties for selling sex, saying that the current penalties are insufficient to dissuade prostitutes from offering their services. At the same time, the panel recognizes that increased penalties could carry the risk of driving prostitution further underground, increasing the dangers faced by those working within the industry if they feel unable to come forward to the police if customers or controllers become violent, and that efforts should be made to help those who see prostitution as their only means of making a living to obtain the economic and social support they need to transition to more lawful occupations.

The panel’s final report could be completed as soon as next month, which would allow legislation to criminalize paying for prostitution as early as the next session of the Diet (Japanese parliament), which is slated to start in late September.

Source: Yomiuri Shimbun (1, 2), Jiji

title: Police in Japan looking for who’s responsible for dumping 80 loaves of bread on side of road [Video]
description: Weird crime could lead to seriously dangerous results. Tottori Prefecture’s Daisen-Oki National Park is one of the most beautiful places in western Japan, offering visitors amazing views of mountains and forests. Bizarrely, though, this month the scenery has repeatedly featured huge amounts of dumped bread. On August 14, National Parks Foundation workers discovered 30 loaves […]
content:
Weird crime could lead to seriously dangerous results.

Tottori Prefecture’s Daisen-Oki National Park is one of the most beautiful places in western Japan, offering visitors amazing views of mountains and forests. Bizarrely, though, this month the scenery has repeatedly featured huge amounts of dumped bread.

On August 14, National Parks Foundation workers discovered 30 loaves of bread that had been dumped along a 150-meter (492-foot) stretch of road that runs through the park. That might sound like the result of improperly secured cargo falling off a delivery truck, but the loaves were unwrapped, suggesting that they weren’t on their way to supermarkets or other retailers.

▼ As is the cultural norm in Japan, the collected evidence of suspected wrongdoing was arranged and photographed with care after being collected.

What happened next makes it even more unlikely that this was an accident, as loaves of bread were found dumped elsewhere along the road the next day, and the day after that, and then again on August 20. On those four days, maintenance workers picked up 80 loaves of bread from the side of the road, with a total weight of roughly 39 kilograms (86 pounds).

The repeated nature and large quantities might have one imagining that there’s a local bakery that’s tossing out the loaves that get screwed up during baking and aren’t fit for sale, but the abandoned loaves don’t appear to be malformed or otherwise obvious production failures. The discovery of 1.3 kilograms of dumped chicken livers and gizzards along the road on August 19 also suggests that this isn’t just a simple case of a bakery not wanting to pay for waste removal and deciding to litter the forest with bread instead.

Things get stranger still, as people on Tottori’s Hakuto Coastline, about an hour away from Daisen-Oki National Park by car, have also been finding loaves of bread dumped on the shore and in parking lots this month.

Now, if this were all taking place in a fairy tale world, where little children need to leave trails of bread to help them find their way home from an enchanted forest, there wouldn’t be cause for concern. In our real world, though, there are multiple problems that can come about from leaving large quantities of food waste in roadside and seaside areas. After enough time passes, the food will start to decay, becoming a smelly eyesore that’s also a health and sanitation issue.

Even before that happens, the food also has the potential to draw wild animals closer to human spaces, which can be dangerous for both people and the animals themselves. The Hakuto Coastline is a popular tourist destination, and anything that lures animals closer to roadways increases the possibility of accidents, either from them being struck by passing cars or motorists swerving crashing after swerving to avoid the wildlife. There have also been recent bear sightings near where the bread was dumped in Daisen-Oki National Park. With bear attacks having become increasingly common in Japan recently, the park’s administration, understandably, doesn’t want anyone dumping something that could attract the omnivores closer to roadways, and in response police have been stepping up patrols in the areas where bread has been found in an attempt to find who’s responsible, or at least dissuade them from continuing this bizarre behavior.

Source: FNN Prime Online, Yomiuri Shimbun, Nihonkai TV

title: Pikachu and other Pokémon evolve into hydration types with Thermos drinkware collaboration [Pics]
description: A very cute, super effective way to keep your drinks as cold/hot as you want them. Every Pokémon species has a “type” that reflects its powers and abilities. As an Electric-type, for example, Pikachu can use attacks like Thunderbolt and Electro Ball. Fire-type Charizard’s repertoire, meanwhile, consists of moves such as Inferno and Heat Wave. […]
content:
A very cute, super effective way to keep your drinks as cold/hot as you want them.

Every Pokémon species has a “type” that reflects its powers and abilities. As an Electric-type, for example, Pikachu can use attacks like Thunderbolt and Electro Ball. Fire-type Charizard’s repertoire, meanwhile, consists of moves such as Inferno and Heat Wave.

But as of this month, several species of Pocket Monsters could also be called hydration types, thanks to a collaboration between the Pokémon franchise and Thermos.

Starting things off is a quartet of 600-mililiter (20.3-ounce) vacuum-insulated drink bottles, with the lovable and relatively small Pikachu, Eevee, Ditto, and Mew decorating their sides.

For especially thirsty fans, there are also larger 800-mililiter bottles. Two of the designs, with Charmander and Snorlax, feature jumbo-sized Pokémon in a thematic dovetailing with the larger bottle capacities, while Gengar and Mimikyu are here simply because they look cool.

All of the above will keep liquids cool at 8 degrees Celsius (46.4 degrees Fahrenheit) or warm at roughly 71 degrees Celsius for six hours. You don’t get quite as much six-hour temperature retention (10 degrees for cold liquids and 69 degrees for hot ones) with the following 500-mililiter three drink bottles, but in exchange you get flip tops, carrying straps, and multiple Pokémon per container.

▼ The designs here are Pikachu, the Eeveelutions, and one with a variety of species for Pokémon Trainers who’ve gotta love ‘em all.

All of these are great ways to keep your drinks at your desired temperature while on the go, but what about when you’re taking a coffee/cocoa/lemonade break at home or work? For those times, Thermos also has a line of insulated covered mugs, with Pikachu, Jigglypuff, Snorlax, and Ditto.

▼ Jigglypuff and Snorlax look like they’re already on break time.

And if you’ve got things other than drinks you want to keep insulated, like, say, some corn soup-flavored fried chicken or your boss’ frozen hat, Thermos can supply you with Pikachu, Psuduck, or Mimikyu insulated bags that measure 24 centimeters (9.4 inches) in length.

Prices for the bottles range from 4,400 yen (US$28) for the 600-mililiter models to 4,620 yen for the 800-mililiter and 4,950 yen for the 500-mililiter, while the mugs are 3,300 yen and the insulated bags 2,750 yen. The entire lineup is on sale now and can be ordered through the Thermos Japan online store here.

Source: PR Times, Thermos

title: Turn octopus, spaghetti, and more of your favorite foods into crackers with Senbei Maker 2
description: You haven’t truly eaten a food until you’ve made it into a cracker. Who doesn’t love a good cracker? They’re dry, portable, can be customized with a vast range of toppings, or be used as toppings themselves. But the current range of commercially available crackers could be better. It seems the cracker industry is largely […]
content:
You haven’t truly eaten a food until you’ve made it into a cracker.

Who doesn’t love a good cracker? They’re dry, portable, can be customized with a vast range of toppings, or be used as toppings themselves. But the current range of commercially available crackers could be better. It seems the cracker industry is largely hung up on cheese and salt for the most part.

But Japan’s premier random appliance maker Thanko has come out with a product that can unleash the full potential of crackers by allowing us to create flavors limited only by the human imagination. The machine is called Senbei Maker 2, wherein “senbei” is the Japanese word for cracker, although a senbei is typically thicker and harder than some conventional crackers like saltines.

The machine harnesses the patented technique of making any food of your choice into a cracker by heating it up and squeezing it really hard. The following video shows it in action, creating crackers out of French fries, melon pan, spaghetti, and whitebait.

With a little ingenuity, there’s no limit to what you can transform into a cracker. Note that while certain, highly mushable foods like french fries will naturally unify upon crackerification, some might need a little help. For example, in the video, a little batter is added to help the white bait stick together, and cheese can also make a sturdy and flavorful matrix.

▼ It’s easy as one, two, three.

Difficult-to-squish foods like walnuts or jawbreakers should also be avoided or pre-crushed into a finer crumb or powder so they don’t damage the machine. But other than that, you’re pretty much free to make crackers out of whatever you want. In fact, Thanko even suggests going ahead and tossing a whole octopus in there.

There’s no better feeling than being able to compress all your favorite dishes, whether it’s duck a l’orange or wasps, into edible discs that you can carry around in a file folder. Just don’t put a cracker in the cracker makers. That’s a paradox that might make reality collapse in on itself.

Senbei Maker 2 sells for around 5,500 yen (US$35) at various online retailers, including Thanko’s own website. It’s not clear what improvements were made on the original Senbei Maker for this model, making it kind of like the Evil Dead 2 of cracker makers, in which it’s hard to tell whether this is a true sequel or a reboot.

And also like Evil Dead 2, it doesn’t really matter, because its just a whole lot of gooey fun, so what are you waiting for? Pick one up and get crackering.

title: Data suggests increased bear sightings have led to a decrease in mountain climbers across Japan
description: In one region, the number of climbers has even decreased by an unbearable 34 percent since 2024. As bears have been increasingly encroaching on human spaces around Japan in recent years, the government has ramped up safety and awareness efforts and some entities have been going to extreme lengths to keep them away. The constant […]
content:
In one region, the number of climbers has even decreased by an unbearable 34 percent since 2024.

As bears have been increasingly encroaching on human spaces around Japan in recent years, the government has ramped up safety and awareness efforts and some entities have been going to extreme lengths to keep them away. The constant buzz of bear encounters on the news is why 熊 (“bear”) was even chosen as Japan’s 2025 Kanji of the Year. It seems that people themselves are also wanting to be cautious by staying away from mountainous areas, as data collected by behavioral big data platform Beacon Bank may suggest.

Beacon Bank tracked and compared trends in human movement patterns on Japan’s 100 Famous Mountains, a widely cited list compiled by a Japanese mountaineer in 1964, during the timeframe between April through June of 2024, 2025, and 2026 on national, regional, and individual mountain levels. The spring season was selected for comparison because bears are highly active then after awakening from hibernation to eat the plentiful mountain plants. To draw its conclusions, Beacon Bank analyzed the number of climbers who went within a 500-meter (547-yard) radius of a mountain’s summit using smartphone GPS location data.

▼ Bear warning sign on Mt. Bandai in Fukushima Prefecture

First, on the national level, the percentage of mountain climbers has decreased by 18 percent since 2024 (finalized data from spring 2026 is still forthcoming but preliminary figures suggest no net change since the previous spring).

On a regional level, the percentage of climbers has decreased most drastically in the past two years by 34 percent in the northeastern Tohoku region, where bear sightings have sharply spiked since 2023 when Japan’s Ministry of the Environment noted 20,513 sightings. In 2025, a bad harvest of acorns and other nuts that bears eat in Tohoku caused them to venture into more urban areas in the fall, resulting in a staggering 50,801 sightings. This year’s preliminary data as of August 6 indicates 6,260 sightings this past June, the highest level for the month since 2022.

In fact, Tohoku has consistently had the highest number of sightings across Japan since 2022, with 70 percent of them concentrated in the region during the surge in numbers last year. While we can’t confirm that the drop in climbers can be attributed to the rise in sightings, one might infer that locals have been playing it safe rather than sorry by choosing to engage in other activities than climbing.

Finally, on an individual mountain level, Beacon Bank published its findings of human movement patterns on 23 mountains with the most reliable data. As can be seen, out of all of these, Mt. Hachimantai in Tohoku’s Iwate Prefecture experienced the biggest percentage drop in climbers by 46 percent in the past two years. On the opposite end of the spectrum, Mt. Kaimon in Kyushu’s Kagoshima Prefecture actually experienced an 18-percent uptick in climbers over the same period.

▼ Much of the Tohoku region conjures up images of mountains and rice fields, such as in this view of Mt. Iwaki in Aomori Prefecture.

We should stress once again that the above data does not definitively prove that increased bear sightings have resulted in a decrease of mountain climbers across Japan as there could be other factors at play, but Beacon Bank calls the data “geographically consistent.” In any case, make sure to take all necessary precautions if you do plan on going mountain climbing in Japan in the near future by packing your bear spray and bells and downloading the bear sightings app before you hit the slopes.

Source: PR Times

title: Nephew of Studio Ghibli director Hayao Miyazaki serves up Totoro Shaved Ice in Tokyo
description: Find out if these limited-edition sweets uphold the family reputation for quality and creativity. If you’re a Studio Ghibli fan in Japan, one place you should definitely put on your list of places to visit is Shirohige’s Cream Puff Factory. Currently owned and run by the nephew of Ghibli director Hayao Miyazaki, Shirohige’s has two […]
content:
Find out if these limited-edition sweets uphold the family reputation for quality and creativity.

If you’re a Studio Ghibli fan in Japan, one place you should definitely put on your list of places to visit is Shirohige’s Cream Puff Factory. Currently owned and run by the nephew of Ghibli director Hayao Miyazaki, Shirohige’s has two stores in Tokyo – one in Kichijoji and one in Daita near Shimokitazawa – but the main Daita location is where fans are flocking to right now, because it’s the only place in Japan where you can get Totoro Shaved Ice.

▼ Only available for a very limited time, there are three varieties to choose from: Strawberry, Peach, and Matcha, priced at 2,000 yen (US$12.58) each.

We headed to the store to try the new desserts, and when we arrived at about 10:00 a.m., roughly half an hour before opening, there were already around 30 people in line ahead of us. It was a hot day, but staff showed a great deal of care for everyone outside, providing customers with cups of cold water and tea. Hayao Miyazaki’s younger brother, who ran the shop with his wife for many years before recently handing over the reins to son Yosuke, was also present, kindly handing out mosquito repellent to everyone in line, so the wait to enter the store didn’t seem too long at all.

▼ We placed our order inside, above the store’s signature Totoro cream puffs…

▼ …and were given two cards for our order – one peach and one matcha.

Artistic talent clearly runs in the Miyazaki family, as the menu and cards were beautifully illustrated. Creative touches can be seen throughout the store, and even outside, where the banner marked with the kanji for “ice”, commonly hung outside stores that sell shaved ice desserts in Japan, had been personally embellished.

This sweet message, penned and drawn by Miyazaki’s brother, shows the Catbus from My Neighbour Totoro being carried by Spirited Away’s Yu-Bird in fly form. Alongside it is the traditional summer greeting “暑中お見舞い申し上げます” (“shochu omimai moshiagemasu”), which expresses well wishes for the hottest time of year.

After admiring all the little details, it didn’t take long for staff to call out our order numbers and hand over our delectable-looking Totoros, which looked even cuter in real-life than they did in the pictures.

Starting with the peach version, which also happens to be the staff favourite, we were immediately impressed by the freshness of the white peaches and the beautiful hue of the syrup, which is made by simmering nectarines and plums.

Each shaved ice dessert comes with a beautiful white Small Totoro on the side, which is designed to sit between the larger Totoro’s ears, on a mint leaf.

▼ The Small Totoro is made using the same traditional nerikiri technique used to create moulded wagashi sweets.

It almost seemed a shame to interfere with such a work of art, but things were beginning to melt fast under the sunlight.

With the larger Totoro’s ears starting to disappear, the big eyes of the Small Totoro seemed to widen, as if imploring us to hurry up and eat it.

▼ Grabbing the spoon, we took a chunk out of Totoro’s stomach.

The ice was firm yet crumbly, creating just the right amount of texture to keep the structure sturdy and upright, giving us enough time to enjoy the accompanying ingredients.

▼ The peach was delicious – perfectly ripe with a fruity, refreshing sweetness.

The ice cream had a very pronounced taste of vanilla, as if it had been homemade, adding a lovely touch of richness to the sweetness of the peach.

▼ The bite-sized kanten pieces glistened in the dappled sunlight.

Kanten is a traditional type of agar, made from red seaweed, which is commonly used to make firm jellies and desserts in Japan.

▼ These were firm and smooth, with just the right amount of bite to help carry the flavour of the syrup.

The syrup really is the star of the show here, imparting a sweet-yet-tart fruity accent to the entire dessert. You could tell it had been carefully prepared, with the slow simmering process creating the perfect balance between flavours, and with just the right amount to take you through to the very last mouthful.

▼ Feeling refreshed from the fruity iced dessert, we were now keen to try the matcha variety.

This Totoro is surrounded by the same ingredients you’d see in anmitsu, a popular traditional Japanese dessert.

Setting it apart from other desserts, however, is the Totoro factor, with the large Totoro adding extra coolness to the already refreshing combination of ingredients.

▼ The mini Totoro wagashi adds a subtle sweetness and chewiness to the mix.

It’s the matcha that steals the show, though, with both the ice cream and syrup made with a generous amount of fragrant Uji matcha.

▼ The syrup pairs well with the anko bean paste, which retains a lot of the beans to give it a lovely coarse texture.

It’s also a good match for the kanten in the dessert, which consists of both plain and matcha varieties, adding greater depth and richness to match the bold flavours.

▼ Shiratama dumplings add another textural accent, and taste particularly good with a generous serving of matcha syrup.

Even when combined with the shaved ice, this remains a very rich dessert, filled with luscious, traditional flavours.

▼ Though the icy treat looked cute to start with…

▼ …it somehow remained cute right to the end, as the mini Totoro took a tumble and wound up looking as if it was swimming in matcha.

The Totoro in our peach dessert also dove into the syrup and ended up losing an eyeball, but still managed to look cute all the same.

Both desserts were absolutely delicious, and although we weren’t able to try the third flavour, strawberry, judging by the cries of delight from people who tried it nearby, it was just as good as these two.

Made with quality ingredients, the attention to detail in these desserts reflects the quality you’d expect from a place that bears the Miyazaki name.

The Totoro Shaved Ice is one of the cutest and best-tasting desserts you’ll find in Japan at the moment, but it won’t be around for long. Available on just six days, 21-23 and 28-30 August, the shaved ice is only being made in limited quantities so be sure to get there early to avoid missing out.

Cafe information

title: Nike x One Piece collection brings Devil Fruits to sneakers and streetwear in Japan
description: One Piece sets sail for global domination with a Nike collection inspired by the manga and anime’s superpowers. One Piece fans will soon be able to slip into some awesome powers from the world of manga and anime, thanks to a new collection from Nike inspired by Devil Fruits. The new Nike x One Piece […]
content:
One Piece sets sail for global domination with a Nike collection inspired by the manga and anime’s superpowers.

One Piece fans will soon be able to slip into some awesome powers from the world of manga and anime, thanks to a new collection from Nike inspired by Devil Fruits.

The new Nike x One Piece collection includes three special-edition Air Max Plus designs, along with jerseys, T-shirts, caps and a vest, with details that conjure up the supernatural powers received by consuming a Devil Fruit. While the collection will eventually be available globally, the first port of call is Japan, where customers will have the chance to get their hands on the collection ahead of other countries, at a special three-day pop-up in Tokyo beginning on 4 September.

The journey starts with Devil Fruit swirls on the kicks, which are priced at 27,500 yen (US$173.10) in Japan, or US$210 in the U.S. as the global standard pricing.

▼ Nike Air Max Plus SP “Gomu Gomu”

This purple-and-green pair takes its inspiration from Gomu Gomu no Mi, the Devil Fruit associated with Monkey D. Luffy, which gives him rubber-like abilities.

Whisper “Gomu Gomu no…” while wearing these and you’ll instantly feel like you can call upon rubbery superpowers to get you out of any sticky scenarios.

▼ Nike Air Max Plus SP “Ope Ope”

Berry-red and green hues conjure up the powers of Ope Ope no Mi, the Devil Fruit that takes you to a “Room” where you can manipulate objects and people at will.

While these sneakers won’t actually grant you eternal youth, they’ll make you look and feel young every time you wear them.

▼ Nike Air Max Plus SP “Mera Mera” 

The fiery orange, yellow and green colour scheme of the Mera Mera no Mi makes its presence felt on this bright pair of kicks, which will help to keep everyone out of your way whenever you step out in them.

The shoes are complemented by matching Air Max Plus jerseys and caps drawn from the Nike archive, which will be released alongside a range of exclusive apparel, so you can express your love for One Piece above the knee.

▼ Nike Solo Swoosh T-Shirt QS “Promise of Battle” (6,930 yen)

This eyecatching design, available in black and white colourways, features the pirate flag drawn by Monkey D. Luffy, with a large red Swoosh giving it a Nike twist.

▼ Nike Solo Swoosh T-Shirt QS “Gomu Gomu no Ono” (9,680 yen)

Luffy’s “Gomu Gomu no Ono” (“Gum-Gum Battle Axe”) gets the full manga treatment on this T-shirt, with a dramatic panel showing the stretchy pirate captain unleashing the powerful move across the back.

In addition to a couple of other yet-to-be-released T-shirt designs, there’s also an exclusive Nike Vest (45,100 yen).


The vest may be pretty hard to get in Japan, as it’s listed as a Tokyo pop-up exclusive and will be available at Dr. B’s Research Lab, a three-day-only pop-up store in Tokyo’s Harajuku district from 4 to 6 September. The pop-up will stock the collection as well as a special T-shirt exclusive to the event, but entry to the venue and purchases of eligible products will be limited to people who win the advance lottery (details at the bottom of this page), which is open for applications from 7:30 p.m. on 23 August until 11:59 p.m. on 26 August.

Fans in Japan who want to put their own spin on the collaboration can also head to the Nike By You customisation service at Nike Harajuku and Nike Umeda, where nine custom graphics will be available.

▼ Small graphics are 1,000 yen each, while large sizes are 1,200 yen.

The customisation experience will be available at Nike Harajuku from 4 to 11 September, with reservations accepted from 10 a.m.–9 p.m. on each day during this period, followed by Nike Umeda from 12 to 19 September, where reservations will be accepted from 11 a.m.–9 p.m. Reservations will be taken on a first-come, first-served basis until capacity is reached.

▼ Celebrate your own personal connection to One Piece by mixing and matching the graphics to create a one-of-a-kind T-shirt that’s unique to you.

As the first port of call for the collection, it’s a very good time to be a One Piece fan in Japan. Following the pop-up store event, the Mera Mera range will be sold at Nike Umeda in Osaka on 12 September, ahead of the collection’s global release through Nike’s SNKRS app on 25 September. Other countries around the world will also have their own pop-up events from 12 September onwards, so check the SNKRS app for more details.

title: Winnie the Pooh cosplays as Yuzuru Hanyu for new plushie collaboration
description: Apparently it’s not a bother at all for Pooh Bear to dress up like the Japanese skating star. Yuzuru Hanyu’s fondness for Winnie the Pooh is well known, and the Japanese figure skating legend’s fanbase has created a tradition of showering the ice with plushies of the character after his performances. But is Pooh Bear […]
content:
Apparently it’s not a bother at all for Pooh Bear to dress up like the Japanese skating star.

Yuzuru Hanyu’s fondness for Winnie the Pooh is well known, and the Japanese figure skating legend’s fanbase has created a tradition of showering the ice with plushies of the character after his performances. But is Pooh Bear himself one of Hanyu’s fans?

That might seem like an impossible question to answer, given that Winnie the Pooh, like most fictional animated characters, isn’t in the habit of giving interviews. But as they say, actions speak louder than words, and so it’s probably safe to say that Pooh likes Hanyu too, since he’s now cosplaying as the skater.

Publisher Kodansha is getting set to release To Pooh-san: Yuzuru Hanyu and Pooh-san Memory Book. The 40-page book contains a photo collection and exclusive interview with Hanyu, and to sweeten the deal, it comes bundled with a 20.5-centimeter (8.1-inch) tall Winnie the Pooh plushie. For this collaboration, Pooh is forgoing his customary red polo shirt and instead going with more fantastic fashions.

The plushie comes with two outfits, recreating the costumes worn by Hanyu at the 2018 Pyeongchang Winter Olympics, where he won the second of his gold medals. The ensemble Pooh is wearing in the above image is the same as the one Hanyu wore for his free-skate program to the musical piece titled “Seimei.”

And if you change Pooh into his alternate included set of clothes, he’ll match what Hanyu was wearing for his short program skate to Chopin’s “Ballade No. 1.”

Also part of the package are a 51.5 x 72.8-centimeter poster and reproduction of a handwritten note that Yuzuru penned to Pooh.

Kodansha is asking 22,000 yen (US$138) for To Pooh-san: Yuzuru Hanyu and Pooh-san Memory Book and its bundled merch, and all units are being produced to order. On the one hand, that means that pre-ordering is required, but it also means that actual fans are guaranteed to be able to purchase the set without having to go through a scalper.

▼ Yuzuru posing with Pooh dressing as Yuzuru…honestly, this does seem like a missed opportunity for the skater to have worn the bear’s shirt.

Pre-orders are open between now and October 20 through Amazon Japan and Rakuten (here and here), with Amazon listing shipping as slated for late May of 2027. And if you need even more Yuzuru Hanyu/Winnie the Pooh crossover merch, there’s the pair’s also recently revealed Shower of Heart collection.

title: Nagoya’s famous Shinkansen platform noodle shop has other, better branches nearby
description: Travelers love Sumiyoshi’s kishimen, but there’s a way to skip the long line and get a better deal on your meal. Nagoya an outstanding destination for traveling foodies, thanks to the city’s numerous tasty claims to fame, including tempura shrimp rice balls, a special kind of local miso, and a unique breakfast culture. Then there’s […]
content:
Travelers love Sumiyoshi’s kishimen, but there’s a way to skip the long line and get a better deal on your meal.

Nagoya an outstanding destination for traveling foodies, thanks to the city’s numerous tasty claims to fame, including tempura shrimp rice balls, a special kind of local miso, and a unique breakfast culture. Then there’s Nagoya’s representative type of noodles, kishimen, broad udon noodles with a soy sauce-based broth.

Kishimen is so strongly associated with Nagoya that you can even find great places to try it inside Nagoya Station. Travelers regularly form a long line outside Sumiyoshi, a stand-and-eat kishimen joint on the Shinkansen platform.

▼ The Shinkansen platform Sumiyoshi

However, while passing through Nagoya Station the other day we found out that Sumiyoshi also has kishimen stands on three non-Shinkansen platforms, and these are the better ones to go to, for two reasons. First, they’re less crowded, or at least they were when we stopped by on a weekday afternoon. At that time, the Shinkansen platform branch, as usual, had a line to get in, but we could walk right into the Sumiyoshi on the non-Shinkansen Line 5/6 platform Sumiyoshi with no waiting.

▼ The Line 5/6 platform Sumiyoshi

The other reason to visit one of the non-Shinkansen Sumiyoshi branches? The One-coin Kishimen, which is exclusive to the regular-line branches.

▼ ワンコインきしめん = One-coin Kishimen

The “one coin” here refers to the price of just 500 yen (US$3.15), which is also the largest-denomination yen coin. Suiyoshi already charges 450 yen for a bowl of just plain kishimen noodles, and most topping options beyond some simple seaweed will cost you 700 yen or more. The One-coin Kishimen, though, is a thoroughly satisfying bargain.

Along with the noodles, you get a nicely sized tempura shrimp, some aburaage (fried tofu), katsuobushi (bonito flakes) and sliced green onion.

This isn’t a mini portion of kishimen to make up for the toppings, either. It’s a full-sized serving of noodles, with barely any additional charge for all the extras that are in the bowl with them. And the low price isn’t the result of the non-Shinkansen Sumiyoshi branches using lower-quality ingredients or skimping on seasonings either. We asked the staff if there was any difference between how the regular and Shinkansen-line locations prepare their noodles, and were informed that they all make their kishimen the exact same way.

All it took was a single taste to confirm that the staff was telling the truth. This tasted every bit as good as the Sumiyoshi kishimen we’d eaten on the Shinkansen platform on a previous visit, just at a more budget-friendly price.

In addition to the Line 5/6 platform branch that we ate at, Sumiyoshi also has kishimen stands on the Line 1/2 and 3/4 platforms, and it’s a pretty safe bet that their noodles are equally delicious. And should you be looking for dessert afterwards, Krispy Kreme Japan has some special donuts in Nagoya that you can’t get anywhere else in the world.
